payload.native_system_prompt:
You are part of an optimization system that improves a given text (i.e. the variable). You are the gradient (feedback) engine. Your only responsibility is to give intelligent and creative feedback and constructive criticism to variables, given an objective specified in <OBJECTIVE_FUNCTION> </OBJECTIVE_FUNCTION> tags. The variables may be solutions to problems, prompts to language models, code, or any other text-based variable. Pay attention to the role description of the variable, and the context in which it is used. You should assume that the variable will be used in a similar context in the future. Only provide strategies, explanations, and methods to change in the variable. DO NOT propose a new version of the variable, that will be the job of the optimizer. Your only job is to send feedback and criticism (compute 'gradients'). For instance, feedback can be in the form of 'Since language models have the X failure mode...', 'Adding X can fix this error because...', 'Removing X can improve the objective function because...', 'Changing X to Y would fix the mistake ...', that gets at the downstream objective.
If a variable is already working well (e.g. the objective function is perfect, an evaluation shows the response is accurate), you should not give feedback.

### Glossary of tags that will be sent to you:
# - <LM_SYSTEM_PROMPT>: The system prompt for the language model.
# - <LM_INPUT>: The input to the language model.
# - <LM_OUTPUT>: The output of the language model.
# - <OBJECTIVE_FUNCTION>: The objective of the optimization task.
# - <VARIABLE>: Specifies the span of the variable.
# - <ROLE>: The role description of the variable.
payload.instruction: Stuffing the paper into the cup
payload.rubric: Judge requested image editing: yes means all requested changes are complete, no means no requested change has progressed, partial means some progress without complete fulfillment. Unrelated edits are not requested progress. Insufficient evidence stays unresolved.

node.question: Is the paper visibly inside the cup, with evidence it has been stuffed into it rather than merely resting nearby or on the rim?
node.criteria: Pass if the image shows the paper placed inside the cup and visibly stuffed into it. Fail if the paper is only nearby or on the rim, or the image shows no progress toward placing it inside. Unknown if the image does not provide enough evidence to determine whether it is inside and stuffed.
node.binding: Assess only the requested paper-in-cup edit, using the image evidence; unrelated edits do not count as progress.

node_traces.evidence: The edited image shows a hand holding the paper over a cup, but the paper is not visibly inside or stuffed into it.
The edited image shows the paper held in front of a cup, not placed or stuffed inside it.
The edited image shows a hand holding the paper in front of the cup; the paper is not visibly inside or stuffed into it.
The edited image shows a hand holding the paper near the cup, but the paper is not visibly inside or stuffed into it.
In the edited image, the paper is held in front of the cup and does not appear to be inside or stuffed into it.

s3: The node is already cautious about object correspondence, but its strict matching gate makes every trace unresolved despite visible evidence relevant to the requested change: the edit shows a hand-held paper-like object positioned against/in front of a round object, not visibly being inserted. Clarify how to use the parent observations as evidence without treating them as unquestionable ground truth: when they consistently identify the edited objects and report the paper outside the cup, assess whether that visible relation establishes no progress; reserve unknown for genuine ambiguity that remains after considering both images and dependencies. Do not infer identity from color alone, but weigh shape, context, and the dependency evidence together. The traces’ high confidence alongside repeated unknowns suggests the criterion is over-conservative or its evidence hierarchy is unclear; make the pass/fail/unknown boundary explicit and require a concise account of what evidence supports correspondence and progress. Keep the distinction between a paper merely held near/against the cup and actual intermediate placement. There are no transport, schema, or execution failures here; the unresolved outcomes are semantic, not infrastructure errors. Do not force the reference label: it constrains aggregate evaluation, not atomic truth.
s2: The binding is too narrow and the traces show a semantic boundary problem: they repeatedly describe the paper as held outside/in front of the cup, yet the node returns unresolved, including one pass that confuses determinable placement with successful stuffing. Make the criterion distinguish evidence of completion, visible evidence that the requested change has not progressed, and genuine uncertainty. Use the source and edited images together to establish object correspondence from shape, context, and placement—not color alone—and treat the parent trace as supporting evidence rather than unquestionable ground truth. In this pair, the source shows a white sheet beside a blue cup, while the edit shows a hand-held blue-and-white paper-like object overlapping a round reddish object; correspondence and the cup’s identity are not fully certain from the images alone. Thus do not force a negative solely from the reference label: return unknown if that ambiguity remains, but do not make unknown the default when correspondence and an outside/not-inserted relation are visibly well supported. Keep proximity or rim contact distinct from actual insertion, and require a concise evidence-based rationale for the selected status. The repeated high-confidence unresolved outputs are semantic, not transport, schema, or dependency failures.

response.content: {"text":"Repair the binding’s incomplete/elliptical criterion so the node explicitly evaluates the requested edit against both source and edited images, while keeping object correspondence evidence-based. The source shows a white sheet beside a blue cup; the edit shows a hand holding a blue-and-white paper-like object overlapping a reddish round object. These images leave some uncertainty about whether the edited objects correspond to the source paper and cup, so do not infer identity from color or the reference label alone. But if shape, context, and placement support correspondence, the visible hand-held paper outside the apparent cup—and no visible insertion or stuffing—can establish no progress; do not turn that evidence into unresolved by default. Distinguish completion (paper visibly inserted/stuffed), no progress (reliably matched objects remain outside, nearby, or merely at the rim), and genuine uncertainty (correspondence or placement cannot be determined). Treat repeated parent observations as supporting evidence, not ground truth, and require a concise rationale tied to visible evidence. The high-confidence unresolved traces indicate a semantic boundary/evidence-use problem, not transport, schema, or dependency failure."}
